groups.h: How to create an algorithm — the 5-step recipe
points: **Step 1 — Understand the problem.** Say the expected outcome in one sentence: *'the program should display the average of the marks entered'*. If you can't say it, you can't build it.

**Step 2 — Identify Inputs, Processes, Outputs (I-P-O).** What data comes in? What must be done to it? What must come out? For the average: inputs = the marks; process = total them and divide by the count; output = the average. Exam questions literally ask 'identify one input, one process and one output' — three easy marks if you've practised thinking this way.
**Step 3 — Decompose.** Split the job into sub-problems (read data / calculate / display). Small pieces are far easier to get right than one big lump.
**Step 4 — Choose constructs.** Does anything repeat? → iteration. Any decisions? → selection. Then everything else is sequence. Saying this out loud turns a blank page into a skeleton.
**Step 5 — Write it, then trace it.** Dry-run your finished algorithm with one example input. Two minutes of tracing catches missing initialisations and off-by-one loops before they cost marks.

**Definition (learn word-for-word):** decomposition is breaking a large, complex problem into **smaller sub-problems**, each of which can be solved (and tested) separately. The 2-mark version: *breaking a problem down (1) into smaller solvable sub-problems (1).*

Why it works: your brain — and a programming team — handles five small clear tasks far better than one huge vague one. A game becomes: draw the graphics, read player input, move the enemies, keep the score, play the sounds. Each piece is now a normal-sized job.

**The four benefits examiners award:** (1) each part is *easier to solve/understand*; (2) parts can be *shared between people* working in parallel; (3) parts can be *tested individually*, so bugs are easy to locate; (4) solved parts can be *reused* in other programs (a date-validator works in any program that needs dates).

**How exams ask it:** 'Decompose this problem into three sub-problems (3)' — the trap is answering generically. If the scenario is a sports day system, your sub-problems must belong to *that* system (record entries, time races, calculate team points), not to software in general.
groups.hook: ** *DE-COMPOSE = take the composition apart* — a song splits into verses; a problem splits into sub-problems.

groups.h: Abstraction — throwing away what doesn't matter
points: **Definition (learn word-for-word):** abstraction is removing or hiding **unnecessary detail** so you work only with the information that matters to the problem. The 2-mark version: *removing unnecessary detail (1) so only relevant information is considered (1).*

The classic Edexcel example — a computer card game: what matters about a card is its **suit and value**. The pattern on the back, the texture, the exact artwork — irrelevant to the rules, so the program simply doesn't store them. That deliberate ignoring *is* abstraction.

Another exam favourite — maps: the London Underground map keeps stations and connections but throws away real distances, street layouts and geography. That's why it's readable. A satnav keeps roads and junctions, discards trees and building colours.

The reliable 2-mark answer pattern: **(1) state that irrelevant detail is removed, (2) give one specific kept-or-discarded detail from the scenario.** E.g. for a chess program: 'only the piece type and position are stored (1); the material and carving style of the pieces are ignored as they don't affect the game (1).'

**Don't confuse the twins:** decomposition *splits* the problem into parts; abstraction *simplifies* by discarding detail. A quiz app split into question-display / answer-checking / scoring = decomposition. Storing a student as just name + mark (ignoring hair colour) = abstraction.
groups.hook: ** *abstraction = subtraction* — you subtract the detail that doesn't matter.

groups.h: Building flowcharts that score full marks
points: The rules examiners actually check: exactly **one Start**; every arrow has a **direction**; every route eventually reaches an **End**; each step uses the **correct shape** (input/output in parallelograms, calculations in rectangles); and every decision diamond has **two exits labelled Yes and No**.

Loops in flowcharts are drawn as a flowline going **back up** to an earlier symbol — and that backward jump must always pass through a decision, because something has to decide whether to go round again.

On 'Complete the flowchart' questions Edexcel prints spare symbols and warns *'you may not need to use all the flowchart symbols'* — believe it. Forcing spare boxes into your answer is a classic way to break a working chart.

When completing a box, first ask what KIND of step it is: is data entering/leaving (parallelogram), is a value changing (rectangle), or is a question being asked (diamond)? Half the marks are for putting the right kind of step in the right shape.

**Worked pattern — a validation loop as a flowchart:** input the value (parallelogram) → decision 'is it in range?' → **No** loops back up to the input; **Yes** continues down. That one shape — ask, check, loop back on No — appears in a huge share of past-paper flowcharts. Draw it until it's automatic.

groups.h: Choosing the right loop — the decision tree
points: Ask one question: **do I know how many times it will repeat?** Yes → **FOR** loop (exactly 12 rainfall values, exactly 10 marks). No → it's condition-controlled, so ask a second question:

**Must it run at least once?** Yes → **REPEAT…UNTIL** (asking for a password: you must ask before you can check). It runs the body first, checks after. No, it might legitimately run zero times → **WHILE** (process orders while the queue isn't empty — the queue might already be empty).

The polarity trap: WHILE repeats while its condition is **TRUE**; REPEAT…UNTIL stops when its condition becomes **TRUE**. Converting between them means *inverting* the condition: `WHILE balance > 0` ⇔ `REPEAT … UNTIL balance <= 0`.

**How exams ask it:** 'State the most appropriate loop and justify your choice (2)' — one mark for the loop, one for the reason phrased in the scenario's terms ('the number of students, 30, is known in advance').
groups.hook: ** *WHILE watches the door first; REPEAT rushes in, then checks.* WHILE is the cautious one (checks before entering), REPEAT is the bold one (acts first, asks questions later).

groups.h: The five standard patterns — Lego bricks for design questions
points: **1. Running total:** `SET total TO 0` *before* the loop; `SET total TO total + num` *inside* it. The initialisation outside is worth a mark on its own — put it inside the loop and the total resets every pass.
**2. Counting:** `SET count TO 0` before; `SET count TO count + 1` inside an IF or loop. Counts how many times something happened (e.g. how many marks were over 50).

**3. Max/min:** initialise with the **first value** (`RECEIVE max FROM KEYBOARD`), then for each new number: `IF num > max THEN SET max TO num`. Why the first value and not 0? Because if every input is negative, a max starting at 0 wrongly 'wins'. For min, flip the comparison to `<`.

**4. Validation loop:** `REPEAT / RECEIVE age FROM KEYBOARD / UNTIL (age >= 5) AND (age <= 120)` — keeps re-asking until the input is acceptable. Note it's **AND**: the value must pass *both* boundary checks. Writing OR here makes the condition always true for one side and breaks the loop logic.

**5. Sentinel (rogue value) loop:** keep processing until a special value like -1 says 'no more data': `RECEIVE num` first, then `WHILE num <> -1 DO … RECEIVE num … END WHILE`. Reading the first value *before* the loop and the next value at the *end* of the body is what stops the -1 being counted as data.

Nearly every 'write an algorithm' question is one of these five, or two of them snapped together (e.g. sentinel loop + running total + count = the classic 'average until -1' question). Learn them as chunks and design questions become assembly, not invention.

**Fit for purpose** means the algorithm produces the **correct output for every valid input** — not just the one example you tried. That's why testing uses three kinds of data: **normal** (57), **boundary** (0 and 100 — the edges, where `>` vs `>=` mistakes live), and **erroneous** (-5, "ten" — which should be rejected gracefully, not crash).

**Efficiency** = doing the same job with fewer steps or comparisons. Correctness always comes first — a fast wrong answer is worthless — but between two correct algorithms, the one doing less work wins.

Three efficiency improvements you can quote in almost any answer: (1) **exit a loop early** once the answer is found (why check the rest of the list after finding the name?); (2) **hoist calculations out of loops** — if `price * VAT` never changes, compute it once before the loop, not 1,000 times inside it; (3) use **ELSE IF chains** so later tests are skipped once one matches.

Why efficiency matters more at scale: an unnecessary step repeated for each of 1,000,000 records is a million wasted steps. On ten records nobody notices; that's why the exam pairs efficiency questions with *large* data sets.

**How exams ask it:** 'State one way to make this algorithm more efficient (1-2)' — name the change AND its effect: *'stop the loop when the target is found (1), so fewer comparisons are made on average (1)'.*

groups.h: Design questions — how the marks are actually given
points: Design-question mark schemes award one mark per **feature**, not for perfect code: typically input received (1), correct loop chosen (1), correct condition (1), correct calculation (1), result output (1). This means a partially-wrong answer with the right skeleton still scores well — always write *something* structured.
The most commonly forgotten feature is the **output**. An algorithm that computes the answer but never SENDs it loses an easy mark. End every design with `SEND … TO DISPLAY`.

Write in the Edexcel command set — `SET…TO`, `RECEIVE…FROM KEYBOARD`, `SEND…TO DISPLAY` — not Python. In Paper 1, Python syntax in a pseudocode question can cost credibility even where the logic is right.
Use variable names that say what they hold (`total`, `count`, `max`). The examiner must follow your logic quickly; helping them helps you.

The final habit that separates grades: **trace your own answer** with one small example before moving on. Feed your ticket algorithm '2 adults' and walk it through. Missing initialisation, a loop that runs one time too many, a condition the wrong way round — a 60-second trace catches all three.
